title: Type 1L Cement & Concrete Index
summary: A living index of standards, research, guidance, field experience and news on Type IL portland-limestone cement (ASTM C595 / AASHTO M 240, 5-15% limestone) and concrete made with it. Updated daily.
summaryText: Type IL is a binary blended cement with more than 5% and up to 15% limestone, designed for 1:1 replacement of ASTM C150 Type I/II with similar 28-day strength and about 8-10% lower carbon footprint. It is accepted by essentially all state DOTs and became the dominant U.S. cement by 2024. The main practical issues are finishing and setting behavior in flatwork, source-to-source variability, sulfate (thaumasite) exposure, and the 2026 C595 revisions that broaden blended cement composition.

topics.name: Standards and specifications
takeaways: ASTM C595 / AASHTO M 240 (harmonized): Type IL(xx), xx = limestone %; >5% to 15%. Same set and strength limits as portland cement. Suffixes (MS), (HS), (HE), (A).
vs ASTM C150 / M 85: Portland cement allows up to 5% limestone since 2004 (M 85 2007). ACI 225.2 advises listing C595 IL beside C150 Type I, not raising cement content.
Model specs: AIA MasterSpec 03 30 00 and FAA P-501 (EB 106) include Type IL.
2026 revisions: C595-26 adds Type IC (ASTM only), more limestone in IP/IS; IT needs two SCMs.
ASTM work item WK94958 is the revision that bases sulfate-resistant Type IL designations on ASTM C452 testing (R74).
NRMCA's 2026 specification guide (R98) recommends allowing ASTM C595 Type IL rather than mandating a cement type, and notes IL can be qualified as MS or HS.

FHWA-HRT-25-116 (R125, Sept 2025) surveyed 18 commercial PLCs from 13 plants in 9 states: CaCO3 averaged ~10% (estimated limestone ~7–18%); Blaine often poorly correlates with particle-size/reactivity; sulfate optimization is critical for early hydration.
ACA hub (R138) states ACI 318 and ACI 301 include PLCs/blended cements, along with ASTM C94, ICC, FAA and AIA MasterSpec — primary code text still not indexed here.

topics.name: State DOT acceptance
takeaways: Broad acceptance: PCA reports acceptance by 50 states by Feb 2024.
Limestone limits: Nov 2024 survey: only Idaho capped limestone below 15% (12.5%).
IL(HE) emerging: Ohio has a spec section, NYSDOT approved one product, others trialing as Type III replacement.
Approved lists: TxDOT Item 421, Caltrans authorized list (M 240), MnDOT certified sources.
Tighter caps returning: INDOT RSP 901-M-069 (effective Dec 2025) limits limestone in Type IL to 10% by mass of the finished cement, including production tolerance.
NYSDOT's Sept 2026 specs accept Type IL under AASHTO M 240 but require the portland cement in any blend to be Type II or II(MH) (R69); INDOT's 2026 book lists Type IL under M 240 (R70).
SCDOT publishes a dedicated Type IL authorized supplier list (QPL 86, R102).
Oklahoma DOT lists Type IL(10) sources on its cement QPL (Ash Grove Foreman AR & Chanute KS; Amrize/Holcim Ada OK & Midlothian TX) (R131).

topics.name: Carbon, GWP and EPDs
takeaways: About 8% lower GWP: Industry EPDs: PLC (10.8% limestone) is 8.2% lower than portland cement; FHWA cites 8.3%; ACI up to 10%.
Grinding: Extra grinding energy is outweighed by clinker reduction.
New PCR (Oct 2026): ACA is surveying U.S. producers for updated industry-average EPDs, including portland-limestone cement.
Plant-specific Type IL EPDs keep appearing, e.g. Amrize Devils Slide IL(10), issued Feb 2026 (R68).
NRMCA released its Industry-Wide LCA and EPD Version 4 in October 2026 (R99, R100), with PLC included in the modeled cement supply.
Low-dosage (0.3–0.6%) colloidal nanosilica can boost CO2 uptake in Type IL paste; OPC still carbonates more readily, while nanosilica aids PLC via air stabilization and available CH (R127).
ACA blended-cements hub (R138): PLC use since 2021 credited with avoiding over 13.3 Mt CO2; industry-average PLC ~8.2% lower CO2 vs PC per EPDs.
CP Tech/FHWA paving carbon interim guide (R137): Type IL typically ~8–10% lower cradle-to-gate GWP if cement content is not increased; do not raise cementitious content to compensate.

topics.name: Fresh properties and admixtures
takeaways: Higher fineness: Can raise water demand about 1-3 gal/yd3 and reduce bleeding.
Admixtures: Re-tune dosages; avoid over-dosing retarding water reducers; verify air entrainment per source.
Setting: Reports of unpredictable or differential set and top-down crusting in flatwork.

New ASCE JMCE study (R94) of Texas, Colorado and Florida IL cements: lower strength development than Type I/II, higher shrinkage in the first 24 h, but up to 35% higher surface and bulk resistivity; results depended on IL fineness, oxide composition and admixture dosage.

FHWA R125: PLC fineness (PSD more than Blaine) and sulfate balance drive early workability and set; ACI R126 shows set accelerators can support high-early-strength PLC mortars comparable to same-clinker OPC within 24 h.

NCC/TTCC (R136): Braun Intertec testing 10 PLCs (5 companies, 2 plants) for mortar fresh properties (water demand, bleed, set, stiffening) with SCM and WR sensitivity; Fall 2026 NCC presentation planned — complements FHWA-HRT-25-116 (R125).

topics.name: Strength, curing, cold weather
takeaways: Similar 28-day strength: Some field reports of lower early strength and more weather sensitivity.
Type IL(HE): High-early PLC replacing Type III in precast and cold weather.
Cold weather: Standard ACI 306 practice applies; protect until about 500 psi.
Same-clinker PLC can match OPC early (<24 h) compressive strength in HES mortars with set accelerator; SCMs may slow early strength and should be limited based on SCM reactivity tests (R126).

topics.name: Durability
takeaways: Sulfate and thaumasite: PLC alone is more susceptible to thaumasite attack at low temperature; SCMs at sulfate-resisting levels mitigate. Use IL(MS)/IL(HS) or C1012 testing.
Freeze-thaw and scaling: Air, low w/cm, finishing and curing govern; scaling of IL concrete is debated (ACI Point of View).
ASR, chloride: Handled with SCMs as for portland cement; Purdue found PLC-only chloride diffusion up to 30% higher, much lower with fly ash.
Abrasion and carbonation: 2026 Temple study: comparable abrasion when properly proportioned and finished.
Sulfate designation changed in C595-26 / M 240-26: Type IL (MS)/(HS) now based mainly on ASTM C452 14-day expansion (MS at 0.050% max) rather than C1012 (Giannini, CI Oct 2026).

2026 papers add caution for aggressive exposures: PLC paste lost far more mass than OPC in citric acid (R66), limestone concrete deteriorated most under combined sulfate and chloride attack while fly ash held up (R67), and a critical review argues durability, not clinker cut alone, should decide whether limestone-rich binders are truly low-carbon (R65).
A 2026 Revista ALCONPAT review (R101) of nearly five decades of literature finds porosity, chloride diffusion and carbonation rise with limestone content, mitigated by lower w/c and SCMs.
Nanosilica-modified Type IL paste microstructure and carbonation behavior are addressed in ASCE JMCE 2026 (R127); exposure-specific testing remains important.

topics.name: Use with SCMs
takeaways: Synergy: Limestone with aluminous SCMs (fly ash, slag) forms carboaluminates, refining pores.
Ternary mixes: Common in U.S. practice; needed for severe sulfate exposure.
ACA's Sept 2026 contractor article (R97) lays out a five-step vetting workflow (supplier data, targeted testing, mortar screening, concrete testing, field mockups) for blended cements.
Low-grade calcined clay combined with limestone-enriched ASTM Type IL cement is under study for UHPC (R129).

topics.name: Pavements
takeaways: Type IL is widely used in paving; CP Tech and FHWA guides support 1:1 replacement with trial batching (R22, R25, R137).

WDM Iowa forensic (R135): early Type IL urban pavements showed scaling/abrasion and strength scatter linked to construction response (air, water, finish, cure), not an inherent cement defect; practice has reportedly improved.
Crystalline technologies claimed to aid IL pavement durability in Iowa case notes (R134).

topics.name: Precast, floors, bridges
takeaways: Precast and prestressed: PCI Journal 2025 and USDOT research: IL usable in girders; prestress loss and transfer length favorable.
Industrial floors: Comparable abrasion with good finishing and curing.
Tilt-up: Bond breaker compatibility concerns raised with C595-26 compositions.

Shotcrete: ACI Materials Journal 2026 study found PLC wet-mix shotcrete needs more alkali-free accelerator for early strength, with similar 7- and 28-day strength and fiber toughness to portland cement.
3D printing: Early studies use Type IL / GULb binders with cellulose nanomaterials or quarry fines to meet printability.
Type IL is being used in UHPC with limestone-enriched binders and low-grade calcined clay (R129) and in architectural white concrete (IU Ferguson, ~11% limestone PLC; R130).

3D printing (R132, Nature Comm 2026): PLC with additional limestone filler (to ~29–40% LF vs OPC) plus 0.3% cellulose nanofibers improved buildability of overhang geometries vs two commercial printable mixes; TEA/LCA report lower cost and GWP when strength is the functional unit.

topics.name: Mix design guidance
takeaways: 1:1 replacement: Keep cement content; run trial batches and verify fresh and hardened properties.
Adjust: Water within w/cm limit, admixture type and dosage, aggregate grading.

topics.name: Field issues and finishing
takeaways: Bleed and finish: Type IL often bleeds slower; premature finish and water on the surface raise blistering/delamination risk (ASCC Field Guide R10; Euclid contractor guide R133).

WDM forensic (R135): West Des Moines Type IL pavements with scaling/low strength — nothing wrong with Type IL itself; distress tied to high/variable air, mixing, late retempering, finishing and curing responding to different bleed/set. Target ~5–8% air; unit weight at discharge; trial batches/test strips; enforce curing.
Curing and evaporation control matter more when bleeding is reduced (Euclid R93, R133; PACA Oct 2026).
Crystalline admixtures/sealers are being marketed with Type IL for freeze-thaw and chloride resistance (Concrete Products R134; vendor-authored — treat as practice note, not independent research).
Preconstruction evaluation and producer collaboration remain best practice when cement source changes.

topics.name: Supply, producers, adoption
takeaways: Market share: Blended cement about 5% of U.S. market in 2021; about 65 Mt vs 35 Mt portland in 2025 (ACA).
Producers: Examples seen: Amrize, Cemex, Heidelberg, GCC, St. Marys/Votorantim, Illinois Cement.
Variability: Switching IL sources is a recognized concern.

Source-to-source PLC variability is now quantified by FHWA (R125): chemical mill-report values track measured data better than physical (Blaine/density); batch-to-batch early heat of Type IL(10) from one plant varied ≤5%.
NCC Blended Cement Steering (R136): collective SHA request for Type IL plant data (strength, set, fineness, LOI, SO3, limestone) from 2022–mid-2025; analysis ongoing with peer review.

topics.name: Canada and Europe
takeaways: CSA A3001 GUL: Up to 15% limestone since 2008; same requirements as GU; Blaine typically about 100 m2/kg higher.
EN 197-1 CEM II/A-L, B-L: In use in Europe since the 1960s-2000s; may be lower strength class than CEM I, unlike U.S./Canadian equivalence.
GCCA: Treats limestone as a clinker substitute with synergies with other SCMs; flags clay and organic contamination as frost-durability risks.

Nature Comm printable concrete study (R132) cites EN 197-1 allowing up to 35 wt% limestone replacement (vs ASTM C595 Type IL ≤15%); study used PLC plus additional LF, not a commercial EN CEM II/B-L product alone.

topics.name: Research gaps
takeaways: Partly covered: shotcrete (R55); 3D printing now three lab studies (R56, R57, R132) — R132 also gives retail PLC/limestone unit costs in a TEA context.
Partly covered: SCC (R72); mass concrete lab/modeling (R105–R124, R128) but no Type IL field pour with temperature monitoring.
Still open: Type IL ready-mix market cost from a reliable industry source; primary ACI 318/301 code text (R138 is secondary); EN 197-1 official text (only secondary citations).
Microcracking/ITZ imaging in commercial Type IL vs OPC concrete still missing.

topics.name: Microcracking and the interfacial transition zone
takeaways: The ITZ (about 10-50 µm around aggregate) is porous and rich in calcium hydroxide, and microcracks start there first (Mehta & Monteiro; Girboveanu 2021).

Drying shrinkage of the paste is restrained by stiff aggregate, which causes microcracks around aggregates. Crack amount depends on aggregate size, volume fraction and stiffness mismatch (Grassl 2010; Li 2020; Bisschop 2002).
Type IL / PLC: the Purdue JTRP 2025 report found PLC concretes form thinner ITZs than OPC (filler effect), but water reducers raised ITZ porosity and CH build-up in one PLC, weakening it.

Limestone filler: about 5% densifies the ITZ while 10% or more can raise ITZ porosity, and calcite collects at the interface (Ghent; Kotlanova 2021/2022). Limestone surfaces nucleate C-S-H well (Ouyang 2017).
Limestone aggregate can bond chemically with paste at later ages (Mehta & Monteiro). Larger limestone grains showed fewer ITZ microcracks (Golewski 2025).

Methods: micro-CT/3D imaging (Mac 2021), acoustic emission separates aggregate cracks from paste/ITZ cracks (Farnam 2015), DIC at the ITZ (Zhang 2023), fluorescence microscopy for freeze-thaw (Li 2015).
R127 examines Type IL paste microstructure under carbonation with colloidal nanosilica, but still does not provide direct ITZ microcrack imaging comparing commercial Type IL vs OPC concrete.

topics.name: Mass concrete and thermal control
takeaways: FDOT is the clearest Type IL source: Section 346 requires Type IL, IT or II(MH) for mass elements (180°F core max, 35°F differential), and Materials Manual 9.4 Appendix C publishes adiabatic rise tables for Type IL (about 95°F rise at 10 days).

Type IL is not automatically low-heat: finer IL releases more heat in the first 24 h, then less; total heat at 7 days is about 6% lower when dilution dominates (GDOT/Georgia Tech R64; PCA SN3148 R1; PCI Journal R31).
ACI 301 limits mass concrete to 160°F maximum (to avoid DEF) and a 35°F core-to-surface differential.
ACI 207 guides do not address Type IL specifically.
ACI temperature-rise curves trace back to the 1936 Boulder Canyon data; USBR (2015) says correct them for modern cement fineness.
DEF with limestone: carbonate can accelerate DEF after high-temperature curing in lab studies, and fly ash suppressed it (Asamoto 2017); none use commercial Type IL.

A 2026 PINN surrogate (R128) reconstructs full PLC hydration-heat curves Q(t,α) for 0–40% limestone mixtures and can support thermal screening, but it is modeling—not a Type IL field mass-pour case with temperature monitoring.

keyIssues: Finishing and set in slabs: Industry guidance exists (ASCC R10; Euclid R133) but standards for finishing aids are minimal. WDM forensic (R135) links pavement surface distress to finishing/curing response to slower bleed, not a defective cement.

Source-to-source variability: Requalify mixes when cement source changes. FHWA-HRT-25-116 (R125) quantifies commercial PLC composition/reactivity scatter; NCC/Braun Intertec 10-PLC fresh-properties study (R136) due Fall 2026 NCC.
Sulfate and low-temperature exposure: Thaumasite risk without adequate SCMs.
Deicer scaling: Open debate on IL concrete scaling.
C595-26 Type IC and higher limestone IP/IS: Cement type label conveys less about composition.

Early strength: IL(HE) acceptance still emerging at DOTs. ACI Materials Journal (R126) finds same-clinker PLC can match OPC <24 h strength in HES mortars with set accelerator; limit SCMs by reactivity when early strength governs.
State limestone caps: Some DOTs (Indiana at 10%) cap IL limestone below the 15% C595 maximum, so a national IL product may not qualify everywhere.

Aggressive chemical exposure: New 2026 studies show PLC/limestone systems can underperform OPC or fly ash mixes in acid and combined sulfate-chloride exposure, so SCMs and exposure-specific testing matter.

ITZ in PLC: PLC tends to form a thinner ITZ, but admixture interactions and filler levels above about 10% can make it more porous. R127 adds Type IL paste microstructure under carbonation with nanosilica; direct imaging of ITZ microcracks in Type IL vs OPC concrete is still scarce.
Supply and spec drift: some Pennsylvania producers report Type I/II is more available again (PACA, Oct 2026), while NRMCA's 2026 spec guide urges owners not to mandate a cement type.

Mass concrete: Type IL is not automatically low-heat (more heat in the first 24 h), ACI 207 is silent on Type IL, and only Florida DOT addresses Type IL in its mass concrete spec. Keep ACI 301's 160°F max and 35°F differential. PINN heat-curve surrogates (R128) can aid screening but are not a substitute for mix-specific ATR or field monitoring.

changeLog.entry: Added 11 resources (R54-R64): Type IL shotcrete and 3D printing studies, ACA PCR news, GCCA documents, INDOT and IDOT cement specs/lists, Michigan scaling bulletin, NRMCA exposure class guide, USDOT limestone blended cement report. Updated DOT, durability, applications, carbon, international takeaways and research gaps.

Added 10 resources (R65-R74): 2026 durability papers (critical review, citric acid, combined sulfate-chloride), Amrize Devils Slide IL(10) EPD, NYSDOT and INDOT 2026 specs, WACA finishing training deck, ASTM WK94958 work item, plus first SCC and mass concrete sources. Updated durability, standards, DOT, carbon, field takeaways, key issues and gaps.

Added 18 resources (R75-R92) and new topic 'Microcracking and the interfacial transition zone'. Tagged durability, scm, strength and fresh as relevant. Added a key issue and a gap. All entries verified via Crossref or the source pages.

Added 12 resources (R93-R104): ASCE JMCE Type IL source/admixture study, NRMCA 2026 spec guide and Industry-Wide LCA/EPD V4, ACA blended cement contractor article, Euclid curing article, PACA October newsletter, S3 flooring contractor paper, ALCONPAT PLC durability review, SCDOT QPL 86, BYU early-age thesis, Construction Specifier article. Updated field, fresh, carbon, standards, durability, DOT and SCM takeaways, whatsNew and key issues.

Added 20 resources (R105-R124) and new topic 'Mass concrete and thermal control'. Tagged dot, standards, scm, durability, guides, field, intl and gaps where relevant; R1, R31, R64, R73 also linked to the topic. GDOT mass concrete report (R118) has unconfirmed authors/year. Updated gaps.

Added 7 resources (R125-R131): FHWA-HRT-25-116 Portland Limestone Cement Variability TechNote; ACI Materials Journal early-age PLC+accelerator strength/porosity study; ASCE JMCE colloidal nanosilica carbonation of Type I/IL paste; Developments in the Built Environment PINN PLC hydration-heat surrogate; Progress in Engineering Science Type IL UHPC with low-grade calcined clay; ACA IU Ferguson PLC white-concrete case study; Oklahoma DOT Type IL(10) QPL. Updated standards, supply, fresh, strength, mass, carbon, durability, microcracking, apps, scm, DOT, field and news takeaways/resourceIds; refreshed gaps (cost/ACI 318/EN 197-1 still open; mass still lacks Type IL field pour with monitoring).

Added 7 resources (R132-R138): Nature Communications CNF+limestone filler printable concrete (with TEA/LCA and EN 197-1 cite); Euclid Type IL PLC contractor guide; Concrete Products crystalline Type IL article; Van Dam/Wathne West Des Moines Type IL pavement forensic (NCC Spring 2026); Masten NCC Blended Cement Steering/PLC variability update; CP Tech/FHWA cradle-to-gate paving carbon interim guide; ACA Blended Cements hub. Updated field, pavement, apps, carbon, fresh, standards, supply, intl and gaps takeaways/resourceIds; refreshed gaps (3DP and partial cost notes; ACI 318/301 and EN 197-1 primary text still open).

gaps: Field performance data: Lab-to-field correlation and performance-based specs still developing; WDM forensic (R135) is a strong local case that attributes distress to construction response, not Type IL chemistry.
Partly covered now: Shotcrete (one 2026 ACI study) and 3D printing (three lab studies including Nature Comm R132 with CNF+LF).
Partly covered now: SCC (one 2018 dissertation). Mass concrete topic expanded (R105-R124) plus PINN hydration-heat surrogate (R128).

Partly covered: cost — R132 TEA quotes PLC ~$0.16/kg and limestone ~$0.038/kg (2025 e-commerce) for printable mortar; still no reliable Type IL ready-mix market cost series. Primary ACI 318/301 code text and EN 197-1 official text still not found (ACA hub R138 confirms code inclusion secondarily).

Microcracking: R127 addresses Type IL paste microstructure/carbonation with nanosilica, but no direct study yet images ITZ microcracks (SEM, CT, AE or DIC) in commercial Type IL vs OPC concrete, separates limestone aggregate from limestone filler effects in PLC, or applies DIC to PLC. No NIST or FHWA report specific to ITZ cracking in PLC was found.

Mass concrete: no field case study of a Type IL mass pour with temperature monitoring; PINN (R128) is modeling/screening only; no same-clinker adiabatic IL vs I/II comparison other than FDOT; DEF with PLC only in lab studies; no DOT other than Florida addresses Type IL in its mass spec; ACI 207 is silent on Type IL.
